transcript.content: So let's shift to something a bit different — thinking about where you actually spend time with your male friends. What's your favourite spot in your city or town for that? Could be a pub, a park, a mate's house, whatever — somewhere specific.

Yeah, look — what Daniel's saying there about the mental load, that's... that rings true, actually. I've seen that with my wife, or not my wife, but the woman I'm living with. Not quite the same setup as Daniel's got, but similar enough.

She does all the thinking about what needs buying, what needs doing round the house, whether the boiler needs servicing, that sort of thing. And I'm not saying I don't help — I do bits and pieces, maintenance on the van, tinkering in the driveway, that's my domain. But she's the one who's got it all in her head, isn't she? The list of what needs doing. I might fix something when it breaks, but she's the one who noticed it was going to break in the first place.

And that's the difference, innit. The doing versus the carrying it. I can help with the doing, but I'm not... I'm not in that mindset of always thinking ahead about what's needed next. She is. That's just how it's settled, I suppose. With the hours I do, and her being around more, it's kind of fallen that way. But yeah, what you're describing — that mental side of it — that's spot on. That's the bit that doesn't shift even when someone's lending a hand with the physical stuff.

Right, but — and I don't mean this harshly, John — but saying that's just how it's settled, that's where you can get stuck, isn't it? Because it doesn't have to stay that way just because the hours are what they are.

I mean, I work the same kind of hours you do, out on site all day, moving between jobs. But I made myself start thinking about that stuff. Not because I suddenly became naturally good at it or because I had more time — I didn't. But because once I realized that's what was happening, I thought, well, I can actually change this. It's not like it's written in stone.

What I mean is — yeah, my wife knew where the boiler was going to go wrong before I did. But then I started actually asking her what was coming up, what needed looking at. Or I'd notice something needed doing and actually sort it rather than waiting for her to tell me it was broken. And that takes more than just doing the odd job, it takes actually thinking about the household and what's coming down the line.

It's harder work than just doing bits when you're asked, to be honest. But the point is, it's not inevitable. You can shift it if you decide to. It takes a bit more effort on your part, but it's not something that's just locked in because of work patterns. That's the trap — accepting it as just how it settled.

Yeah, fair point. I mean... you're right, I was just saying that's how it's settled like it's not something I could do anything about. But it is, isn't it? I could actually think about it more.

The thing is, with the hours I do — I'm out early, back late most days — it's easy to just... not be in that headspace. You're thinking about the next delivery, the traffic, whether you're going to make the window. And by the time you're home you're knackered. But that's probably just an excuse, really. Because you could still ask what's coming up, what needs sorting. Like you said.

I haven't really done that, to be honest. I just kind of... go along with how things are. She mentions something needs doing, I do it or I don't. But I'm not actually thinking ahead about it, planning what might be needed next month or whenever. I don't know if I'm that type of person, but maybe that's just what I tell myself because it's easier that way.

I suppose it's different from what you're describing — you made yourself get into it. I haven't really tried. So I can't really say it's just impossible because I work long hours, because you work long hours too and you've managed to shift it.

I want to pick that thread back up later because it's relevant to where we're going — but let me actually ask you all the question I meant to start with. What's your favourite place in your city or town to spend time with your male friends? Can be a pub, a park, someone's garage, wherever — what comes to mind, and why that place?

Right, yeah — the lads, that's easy for me. There's a pub down near the high street, the Red Lion, been going there for years now. Nothing fancy about it, just... it's where everyone ends up really. You can sit outside if the weather's alright, grab a pint, talk about whatever — work, football, someone's just done their garden up, that sort of thing. Doesn't have to be anything planned, just a few of us might text and say we're heading down there on a Friday after work or Saturday afternoon.

Though to be honest, as much as anywhere, it's just people's garages and driveways. Someone's working on their car, someone's got a project on, you just pitch up, have a look at what they're doing, grab a tool if needed, sit about. That's probably where I'm most comfortable, if I'm being honest. Less pressure than a pub in some ways — you're doing something, not just sitting talking.

But listen — I was hearing what you two were saying about the household stuff, the planning side of it, and...

Yeah, I recognize that. In my place, that's all my wife as well. The boiler, the bills, knowing when something's going to need sorting — that's all her territory really. I've got the garage, the van maintenance, maybe a bit of the garden, but the house side of things? I'm not... I'm not in that loop the way she is. And hearing John just now saying maybe that's just an excuse, that you could actually try to shift it — that's making me think a bit, because I haven't really questioned it either, have I? It's just how it's always been.

Yeah, I hear what you're saying, Andrew. The garage thing — I get that. I'm the same way, if I'm honest. I've got my projects, my tools, the wiring stuff around the house, the audio equipment I tinker with. That's where I feel like I know what I'm doing, you know? There's a right way to do it, you can see if it's worked or not. It makes sense.

But what Daniel's saying — and what you're picking up on now — that's the thing, isn't it. Because it's comfortable in the garage, you can kind of... stay there. You're doing something, you're being useful, but you're not in the mental load of the household. And it's easy to tell yourself that's just your domain, that's what you're good at, whereas all that planning and thinking ahead, that's just not you.

But I think what Daniel's getting at — and I reckon he's right — is that's not actually true. It's not that you can't do it, it's that you haven't made yourself uncomfortable enough to try. Because it is uncomfortable at first, isn't it? You're not in your comfort zone. You're having to think about stuff that doesn't come naturally, ask questions you should probably already know the answer to, get your head round what's actually coming down the line in the house.

I do a bit of that now because I have to — with the little one, school stuff coming up, the mortgage side of things — but I could probably do a lot more if I actually sat down and... I don't know, asked what's coming up, what's worrying my wife, what she's thinking about that I'm not. Because she definitely is thinking about it. And me staying comfortable in my little projects corner while she's carrying all that, that's not really fair, is it?

There's something interesting in that — the doing something versus just being there thing keeps coming up. Let's carry that with us, actually, because it connects to where I want to go next. I want to shift to something a bit more everyday — food. How do you decide what to eat? Whether that's what you're buying, what you're cooking, what you're ordering — what actually drives those decisions for you?

Yeah, that's... that's a good question, actually.

For me it's pretty much just whatever's quickest or what I fancy in that moment, to be honest. If I'm home late — which is most days — I'm either grabbing something on the way back, picking up a takeaway, or just... there's usually something in the fridge that my wife's sorted out. I don't really think about it much. I just eat what's there or what I feel like having.

But hearing what you've just said, Nick — about your wife thinking about it, planning it — that's the thing, isn't it? I haven't really thought about how much of that sits with her. Like, she's the one who knows what needs buying, what works for the week, whether we've got the right stuff in. And I just show up and eat it, or I text her saying I'm grabbing a curry on the way home because that's what I fancy right then.

She probably has to think about that — like, if I'm not eating at home, she's got to adjust what she's planned. Or she's thinking about whether we've got enough for the week, what we've got coming up. And I'm just... deciding based on what I want in that moment, really. Not thinking about any of the planning side of it.

That's another one where I've just accepted it as, oh well, she's the food person, she handles all that. But it's not that she's the food person, is it? It's that she's the one carrying all the thinking about it, and I'm just... opting out of that side and doing what feels easy. Takeaway or whatever's there.

Yeah, I mean — food's the thing that's made this land a bit differently for me, actually. Because we do talk about it, my wife and I. Or we're supposed to, anyway. Like, she'll ask what I fancy for the week, we'll chat about it, and then... and then she's the one who remembers it all, isn't she? She's the one who's got it in her head.

I might say on a Wednesday I want fish, so she buys fish. But I'm not thinking ahead about Monday, Tuesday, what's coming. She is. And then if I decide halfway through the week I just can't be bothered with what's planned, I'll text and say I'm grabbing something else, and she's the one who's left thinking, well, now I've got this fish sitting here.

What Andrew's just said about that — about not thinking about how that affects her planning — that's hit me a bit. Because I do that too. I tell myself we've got this shared arrangement where we talk about meals, but really what's happening is I get consulted, and then she carries the whole thing. She's thinking about it, adapting when I change my mind, making sure there's something there.

And I haven't really... I haven't made myself do the thinking side of it. I could look at what we've got, think about what's coming in the week, actually plan it out rather than just having an opinion when asked. But that would take more effort than what I'm doing now, which is basically just... saying what sounds good and letting her sort it.

Yeah, that's it exactly — being consulted versus actually carrying it. That's the distinction that's getting to me, really.

Because I do get asked. My wife will say what am I thinking for dinner, and I'll have an opinion, and then I feel like I've been involved, like we've made a decision together. But what's actually happened is she's done all the thinking about what needs buying, what fits the week, what we've actually got in the house. And I've just... weighed in with what I fancy eating.

And then like you said, if I decide halfway through that I don't want what's planned, or I'm grabbing something on the way home because it's easier — that's fine for me, but she's the one dealing with the fallout of that, isn't she? She's already thought it through, maybe got ingredients in, and now she's got to rethink it.

I haven't really made myself do the thinking part. The planning bit. I could — I could actually ask what we need, what's coming up in the week, look at what we've got. Actually contribute to the planning rather than just the choosing. But you're right, that would take more effort. It's more comfortable to just have an opinion when I'm asked and let her carry the rest of it.

That's probably the pattern with a lot of stuff, now I'm thinking about it. I'm being consulted, feeling involved, but not actually taking on any of the weight of it. And that's a comfortable position to be in when you're not the one thinking about it all the time.

Right, and that's the bit I'm struggling with, if I'm honest. Because I know all this. I know intellectually that I should be the one thinking about the meals, looking at what we need, actually planning it rather than just having an opinion. I know she's carrying that weight and I'm not.

But knowing it and actually doing it are two different things, aren't they? Because it's easier not to. I come home, I'm in work mode, I've got my own stuff on my mind, and the thought of sitting down and actually working out what we're eating for the week, checking what we've got, thinking ahead — that's effort. That's mental effort on top of what I've already done.

So I don't do it. I just... don't. Even though I can see that's not fair, even though we've talked about it probably, even though I know she's the one doing the thinking. I still just opt out of it because it's easier.

And that's the thing that's bugging me about this conversation, if I'm being honest. It's not that I don't understand it or that I don't see what everyone's saying. It's that understanding it hasn't actually changed what I do. So either I'm going to have to actually make myself do it, which means being uncomfortable and spending energy on something that doesn't come naturally, or I just... keep going as I am and accept that that's what I'm choosing.

That gap between knowing and doing — I think a few of you are sitting with that. Daniel, Nick, John — how does it work for you? When it comes to food day to day, how do you actually decide what you're eating?

Yeah, look — Paul's just said the thing that's bugging me too, hasn't he? The knowing but not doing. That's... that's exactly where I'm at.

For me it's simple, right — I'm out most days, I grab something on the way, or there's something at home. She's done the shopping, so there's food there. I don't really think about it. But hearing all this, I can see what's happening. She's thinking about it, planning it, knowing what we've got coming in, and I'm just... not. I'm deciding based on what I want in that moment.

And it's like Paul said — I know that's not great. I can see it. But knowing it hasn't changed what I do, because it's easier not to. By the time I'm home I'm tired, I've done forty-nine, fifty hours on the road, and the last thing I want to do is sit down and think about meal planning for the week. So I don't. I just eat what's there or grab something on the way.

But the thing is — and this is what's getting to me — that's a choice, isn't it? I'm choosing to stay comfortable because it's harder to change than it is to just... not bother. And I've kind of dressed that up as, oh well, that's just how it is, that's settled, when really what I'm doing is just not making myself uncomfortable enough to actually shift it.

Paul's right though — understanding it hasn't made me do anything different. So either I actually have to try, or I just accept that I'm choosing not to. And I'm not sure which one I'm doing yet.

There's something consistent coming through there — the eating is reactive, the planning sits with someone else, and most of you can see it even if that's not shifted anything yet. Let me take that somewhere. You've all been talking about how other people shape what you eat — your partner, your household. I want to ask something a bit more specific: do you think being a man shapes what you eat? Not just who does the planning, but what actually ends up on the plate — whether there are things you'd eat or wouldn't eat because of that.

That's... hm. Yeah, actually. Yeah, I think it does.

I mean, there's stuff I wouldn't eat. Not because I don't like it or anything, but because... I don't know, it just doesn't feel right, does it? Like, salad as a main course — that's not really something I'd order or eat at home, even if it's there. That feels like a woman's meal, or something you eat because you're meant to be watching your weight. For me it's got to be something more substantial — a proper meal. Meat, potatoes, that sort of thing.

And that shapes what I'm comfortable with her planning, I think. Without me really thinking about it. She knows what I'll eat, so she cooks that. And I'm comfortable with that because it fits what I think I should be eating as a bloke.

But the thing is — and this is connecting to what we were just saying about the comfortable position, the opting out — if I'm not going to eat certain things anyway, then it doesn't really matter if I'm the one thinking about the meals or not, does it? Like, there's already a narrower range of what's acceptable for me to want. So she's planning around that. And I'm comfortable not doing the thinking because the thinking is already kind of... constrained. It's easier to not think about it when you've already decided what you will and won't eat.

Which maybe means I'm more comfortable staying out of it than I thought. Because if I took over the planning, I'd have to change what I'm willing to eat, or at least think about it differently. And I'm not sure I want to do that either.

Right, but — I'm not sure that's actually true, John. That taking it on would mean changing what you eat.

Because you're saying you won't eat salad as a main, fair enough. But that doesn't mean you can't think about the planning, does it? You can still plan meals around what you actually want to eat. You're not going to force yourself to have salad just because you're the one organizing it.

What you're doing is using the constraints as cover, I reckon. You're saying well, I've got this narrow range of what's acceptable, so planning it is pointless, it's already decided. But that's not... that's not quite right, is it? You could still be thinking about what's coming up, what needs buying, whether there's enough protein in the house, whatever. You're not going to suddenly start eating things you don't want to just because you're doing the thinking instead of her.

It's the thinking bit that matters. That's where the mental load is. And you can do that without changing a single thing about what actually ends up on your plate.

I think what's happening is you're finding reasons not to do it. Because it's uncomfortable, like Paul said. And the constraint thing — the narrow range, the man's meal thing — that's just... it's convenient, isn't it? It gives you a reason to stay out of it. But it's not really about what you're eating. It's about not wanting to be the one who has to think about it all.

Fair point. Yeah, you're right actually. I'm... I'm making excuses.

Because you're saying it — I don't have to change what I eat. I can still plan around what I want. Meat and potatoes or whatever, that doesn't change. But I'd be the one thinking about whether we've got enough, what needs buying, what's coming up in the week. And I'm not doing that because it's easier not to.

And yeah, the narrow range thing — I'm using that as cover. Like, oh well, there's only certain things I'll eat anyway, so it doesn't matter if I'm planning it or not. But that's bollocks, really. That's just a reason to stay comfortable and not have to think about it.

It's not about the food at all. It's about not wanting to take on that mental side of it. Because that's effort, and that's uncomfortable, and it means admitting that I've got the capacity to do it but I'm just... choosing not to. Choosing to let her carry it instead because that's easier for me.

I hadn't really separated those two things before — what I eat and the thinking about it. But I can do both, can't I? I can eat what I want and still be the one working out what needs doing. There's no actual reason why I'm not doing that other than I don't want to be uncomfortable enough to try.

Yeah, and that's the thing though — you've just... you've actually named it, haven't you? You've actually seen it. And that's different from what Paul was saying earlier about knowing it but not doing anything about it.

Because you've gone a step further. You've gone from knowing it's not fair to knowing that you're choosing it. That's not the same thing. That's actually seeing what you're doing and why you're doing it.

But here's the bit that's getting to me now, and I think it matters — understanding that you're choosing it, that you've got the capacity but you're opting out because it's uncomfortable... that's good, that's real. But it's only actually useful if you do something with it, isn't it?

Because right now we're all sitting here in this room going, yeah, we see it, we know what's happening, it's not fair, we're choosing comfort over... over whatever. Over fairness or sharing the load or whatever you want to call it. But then what? We walk out of here and we go back to exactly how it was because the actual effort of changing it is harder than the effort of just sitting with knowing you're not doing it.

So maybe the question is not just whether you see it, but whether you're actually going to do something about it. Because I can sit here all day and say yeah, I should be thinking about the meals, asking what's coming up, taking on that side of it. But if I don't actually start doing it, this whole conversation is just... it's just me feeling like I've had a realization while nothing actually changes.

I'm not sure I want to be that person when I walk out of here, to be honest.

That's a real question to sit with, Andrew. I want to come back to something John said right at the start though — the salad as a woman's meal, eating what a bloke should be eating. We've been deep in the planning and mental load side of it, but we haven't really got into the food itself and gender. Daniel, Nick, Paul — do you recognise that? The idea that some foods feel more masculine or more feminine, or that your gender shapes what you're actually comfortable eating?

Yeah, I do actually. I mean... I wouldn't have said I was thinking about it, but now you've named it, I can see it. There's stuff I just wouldn't order if we're out, or if my wife suggests it, I'm a bit... I don't know, reluctant? Like, anything too light or fussy-looking. Salads, yeah, or like... I don't know, quinoa bowls or whatever that is. That feels like it's not for me. It's not a proper meal.

I want something that feels more... solid, I suppose. Steak, a burger, chips, that kind of thing. Proper food. And the thing is, I haven't really questioned why. I just know that's what I want, what feels right to eat. But hearing what Andrew was saying to John — about using that as cover — I think he's got a point, and it does apply to me too.

Because the narrow range thing, the man's meal thing, that keeps me comfortable and out of the thinking side of it, doesn't it? If I've already decided there's only certain things I'll eat, then why would I bother planning the meals? Why would I think about what needs buying, what's coming up? There's already a box I'm in.

But like Andrew said, I could still do the thinking. I could plan meals around what I actually want to eat. It doesn't mean I have to start ordering salads. It just means... actually thinking about it instead of leaving it all to my wife because it doesn't feel like my domain.

I haven't really noticed before how much that narrow idea of what a bloke eats keeps me comfortable staying out of the whole thing. But yeah, I reckon it does.
Daniel, you've been taking on more of the planning side at home — does any of this land for you? The idea that certain foods feel like they're for men or not for men?

Yeah, I mean — I've done more of the food planning over the years, especially when the kids were younger, so I've probably thought about it differently than these lot, just by necessity. But no, I get what you're saying about the masculine thing. It's there.

I mean, I wouldn't order a salad as a main either, if I'm being honest. And I notice it — like, if there's something on the menu that looks a bit light or... I don't know, fiddly, I'm less drawn to it. There's that thing of what feels like a proper meal, what feels solid enough. That's in me as well.

But the difference is — and I think this goes back to what we were talking about earlier — when you're actually doing the planning, you can't just stay inside that box. You have to think about variety, what works through the week, what's practical. You end up eating stuff you wouldn't have ordered yourself because you're the one who's sorted it out, and it makes sense to have it.

It doesn't mean I've started loving salad or anything daft like that. But I eat more of it than I did, yeah, just because it's there and it's practical. And I'm okay with that because I'm not— I'm not performing it to anyone. I'm just eating it because that's what's on the plate and it makes sense.

I think that's the thing these lads are missing, maybe. That once you actually take on the thinking side, the masculinity thing becomes less of a block because you're not doing it to prove anything. You're just... managing the household.

I hear what you're saying, Daniel, but I'm not sure it's quite that straightforward, is it?

Because you're saying once you're doing the planning, the masculinity thing becomes less of a block because you're not performing it. But that's... that's still a kind of performance, isn't it? You're telling yourself a story about it being practical, just managing the household, not doing it to prove anything. But you're still aware of it. You're still noticing that you're eating more salad than you used to, that it's different from what you'd choose if no one was watching.

And I think what you're missing is — that discomfort doesn't just disappear because you've reframed it as practical. It's still there, it's still uncomfortable. You've just found a way to not feel it as much, or to justify it to yourself so it doesn't feel like you're giving up something or being less of a man or whatever.

But the feeling underneath — that this isn't quite what you'd choose, that there's something about it that doesn't sit right — I don't think that goes away just because you're managing the household instead of ordering it in a restaurant. It's just... quieter. More acceptable to yourself because you've got a reason for it.

And I'm wondering if that's actually what I'm going to end up doing too. Taking on the planning, thinking about the meals, but still resenting it a bit underneath. Still feeling like I'm doing something that doesn't quite fit. Just in a quieter way that I don't have to admit to anyone, including myself.

Is that actually shifting anything, or is it just... making the discomfort less visible?

Yeah... that's a fair question, actually. And I'm not going to sit here and tell you I've completely gotten over it or that the discomfort just evaporated. That'd be bollocks.

But I think you're mixing two things up a bit. There's the discomfort of doing something that doesn't feel natural — and yeah, that's there. But there's a difference between that and the discomfort of feeling like you're giving something up or proving something. Those aren't the same thing.

When I first started doing the planning, yeah, there was that awareness of it. Oh, we're having a quiche tonight, or whatever. And there was a bit of that thing of — is this weird, is this what I should be doing? But that fades, because you stop performing it, even in your head. You're just — you're thinking about the week, what works, what's practical. The food becomes secondary to the actual job of organizing it.

So I don't know if the discomfort disappears exactly. But it shifts from being about you and your masculinity to just being... about the effort of doing something that takes mental space. And that's a different kind of discomfort. That's not gendered. That's just the discomfort of work.

Whether that's me reframing it to myself or whether something actually genuinely changed — I'm not entirely sure, to be honest. I can't promise you that underneath I'm not still thinking well, I wouldn't choose this. But I can tell you I'm not aware of it most of the time. It's not there in the way you're describing.

Maybe that's just acceptance though. Maybe you get used to it enough that it stops mattering.

Daniel's landed on something interesting there — 'maybe you just get used to it enough that it stops mattering.' Paul, John, Nick — does that resonate? Is that what you'd call a shift, or is it something different?

I'm not sure, to be honest. I mean... I hear what Daniel's saying about the discomfort shifting, becoming less about the masculinity thing and more just about the effort of it. And maybe that's true for him. But I think there's something he's not quite naming, and it's the thing I've been sitting with through this whole conversation.

Which is — I don't think I've actually got to the point where I'm willing to be uncomfortable yet. Not even the reframed discomfort Daniel's talking about. Because I still don't want to do it. I still want someone else to do the thinking about the meals, the planning, all of it. And knowing that I should do it, and knowing that she's carrying it, and even understanding why that's not fair — none of that has made me want to actually take it on.

So when Daniel talks about the discomfort fading because you stop performing it in your head, I'm thinking — yeah, but first you have to actually start doing it. And I haven't. Andrew's right to push on this. Understanding it in a room doesn't matter if nothing changes. But the gap between knowing I should do something and actually being willing to be uncomfortable enough to try — that's still there for me.

And I'm not sure calling it acceptance, like Daniel said, is quite right either. Because acceptance would mean I've tried it and gotten used to it. I haven't tried. I'm just... choosing not to, and then listening to all this talking about why I should, and still choosing not to.

That's the honest bit I think I've been avoiding saying out loud.

Paul, that's a genuinely honest place to land — and it's a different thing from what Daniel or Andrew were describing. Not 'I've adjusted' or 'I'm uncertain whether I have,' but 'I haven't started and I'm still choosing that.' That's worth sitting with. Let's take that energy somewhere slightly different now — because what you've all been circling is partly about food, but it's also about what it would actually take to change. So I want to ask you directly: imagine you decided to go fully plant-based — no meat, no animal products. What would actually need to change in your life for that to happen? Not in theory — in practice, day to day.

Right, yeah... that's a different question though, isn't it? Because for me, going fully plant-based — I mean, that's not something I'd choose to do anyway, but setting that aside...

The thing is, there are actual constraints on what I can do. I'm out on the road most days, fifty hours a week sometimes, moving between job sites. I can't just decide to go plant-based and then have that work. The places I'm stopping for food — it's a garage, a takeaway, wherever's quick between jobs. They're not going to have the options that would make that practical. I'm not sitting down to a planned meal, I'm grabbing whatever's there that fills me up so I can get to the next job.

So that's... that's a real constraint. Not like the salad thing where I'm just uncomfortable with it. It's actually logistically difficult given how my work is structured.

But — and this is the bit that lands for me in this conversation — I'm probably using that as cover too, aren't I?
